Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of three numbers does not change their sum: adding the first two and then the third gives the same result as adding the last two and then the first. In floating-point arithmetic, however, the result of almost every addition must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Different groupings create different intermediate values, so rounding occurs at different points and may discard different low-order bits.

For example, if a very large number is added to a much smaller number, the smaller contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are added together first, their combined value may become large enough to affect the final result. Subtraction through the addition of oppositely signed values can also cause cancellation, making previously insignificant rounding errors relatively important. Special cases such as subnormal values, overflow, and hardware modes that flush tiny values to zero can increase these differences.

Large matrix multiplication exposes this behavior because every output element is computed as a dot product, which is a sum of many products. High-performance implementations rarely accumulate those products strictly from left to right. They divide matrices into tiles, distribute work across processor cores or graphics-processing-unit threads, use vector instructions, and combine partial sums through reduction trees. Changing the tile size, thread count, scheduling, library version, or target processor can therefore change the order in which partial sums are added.

A sequential reduction, a balanced tree reduction, and a parallel reduction may all be mathematically equivalent, yet produce slightly different floating-point answers. Fused multiply-add instructions further affect results by computing a product and addition with one final rounding instead of rounding the product and sum separately. Some accelerators also use lower-precision products or accumulators for speed, which can magnify order-dependent variation.

These discrepancies are usually small in absolute terms, but they can grow with the length of the dot products and become noticeable for ill-conditioned data or sums containing severe cancellation. Consequently, two matrix multiplications using the same inputs may not be bit-for-bit identical when executed with different reduction orders, even when both implementations are correct. This complicates regression testing, distributed computation, and scientific workflows that require exact reproducibility. Reproducibility can be improved by fixing execution and reduction orders, using deterministic library modes, accumulating in higher precision, or applying compensated or reproducible summation methods, though these choices generally cost performance, memory, or both.
